Cape Town Orchestra

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The first city in Africa to boast a professional orchestra for 100 years

Summary:
Sadly, except for Durban, professional orchestras have disappeared around South Africa. Not so in Cape Town. It is the city's most enduring cultural asset, constantly adapting to the needs of a changing society. We provide a brief history over the last 100 years of the orchestra and the stars it has produced. We discover how and why they have managed to survive when local government funding dried up many years ago. The orchestra manages to survive by outsourcing themselves to a variety of genres - musical productions, international acts etc. But one of the orchestras main functions is to develop skills transfers in the communities. They have training initiatives in townships around Cape Town which are benchmark projects. The aim of these projects are to provide employment for youngsters in the future. A gala concert and dinner is taking place at the beginning of November to commemorate, with the release of a new book, 100 years of existence.


Further information:
A major concert will be taking place on the 22nd of October which we will cover. Also playing on this date will be the junior orchestra. Although we have to meet interviewees, the idea is to tell the story through the eyes of one or two teenagers who are in the youth orchestra.

Press Release:


Cape Town Orchestra
The Cape Town Philharmonic Orchestra is the first in Africa to celebrate a centenary. Carte Blanche discovers the secret behind its business plan, endless passion and a search for fresh musical blood in unexpected areas that keep this ensemble 100 years young.


Script:


CAPE TOWN PHILHARMONIC ORCHESTRA

John Webb:
Like many young girls in townships across South Africa, Noluvuyo Nteta from Khayelitsha near Cape Town, dreams of a career that will bring her fame and fortune.

Noluvuyo Nteta:
It’s really exciting and a bit nervous at the same time, because it’s like a very big performance, I mean, for us.

John Webb:
Tension builds as she packs her violin and evening dress, and joins her brother Siyathemba, a fellow musician, and boards a minibus, which will take then them and others from previously disadvantaged communities to the City Hall. Tonight she’ll be performing for the Cape Town Philharmonic Youth Orchestra, established 10 years ago.

This vibrant symphony orchestra is the training ground for the transformation of the Cape Town Philharmonic, which this year celebrates 100 years of the symphonic tradition, making it the oldest in Africa.

Dennis Davis:
It’s one of the great cultural jewels of the city!

Orchestra Attendees:
We embrace the orchestra, we’re faithful followers!

John Webb:
Louis Heyneman has been at the helm of the orchestra for 14 years.

Louis Heyneman:
I just love the fact that we have here an orchestra culture that we kept alive over 100 years.

John Webb:
In February 1914, a mere six months before the outbreak of World War I, Cape Town established its own municipal orchestra with 18 players, the first orchestra in Africa. A symphony orchestra was considered a beacon of high culture, and all cities around the world yearned to have one. Among the many world-famous performers who visited Cape Town was Austrian tenor, Richard Tauber, in 1939, as well as British conductor, Sir Thomas Beecham, in 1948.

Multi-award-winning and internationally known Cape Town composer Peter Klatzow is a staunch supporter of the orchestra and is well versed in its history.

Peter Klatzow:
He transformed that orchestra single-handedly into a world-class orchestra.

John Webb:
Peter is referring to Benito Moni, who became manager of the orchestra in the 1960s.

Peter Klatzow:
He immediately fired the existing conductor and started bringing out a whole lot of guest conductors. All of them improved the orchestra. He also hired quite a few new people and fired quite a few old ones. You could do that in those days.

John Webb:
The orchestra, which now only uses local musicians, would grow into a world-class ensemble, playing host to some of the world’s foremost conductors and soloists. It’s regrouped a few times and it’s had name changes, but now the Philharmonic is an entrenched part of Cape Town’s cultural heritage.

Do you think in the South African context, it’s even more significance that we have an orchestra that’s been able to survive for 100 years?

Peter Klatzow:
All over the world orchestras unfortunately are collapsing, but yes, it is remarkable. You know, there was a time when people regarded it as Eurocentric, and then a whole number of wonderful young black artists, who were classically trained, like Pretty Yende, came to the fore and that kind of gave the lie to the fact that classical music was really for white-ies only.

John Webb:
Cape Town-trained Pretty Yende is of course world-famous now. But with state subsidy and local government funding drying up, it’s been a momentous task to keep the orchestra alive, especially to discover fresh young talent, like Pretty.

Louis Heyneman:
To see an orchestra for all people, for all occasions, that’s important, because all other music will eventually die if there is not a good orchestra.

John Webb:
Louis Heyneman and his passionate team have had to develop a robust business plan to secure the future of the orchestra.

Louis Heyneman:
We can do everything basically. We play for musicals, we play for ballet, we play for opera, and it’s important- our motto is, “An orchestra for all seasons.”

John Webb:
Versatility is the name of the game. Here the Youth Orchestra collaborated with a rap artist, showing how diverse their talents are. And the orchestra has had to adapt to a changing world, as only 20 percent of money needed comes from ticket sales.

It’s fortunate to have a dedicated group of supporters, Friends of Orchestral Music, fundraising to keep this jewel of the city intact.

Dennis Davis:
It’s actually got an unbelievable outreach program. Young, black kids are gonna be taught to play the violin and other instruments that they want to play.

John Webb:
Noluvuyo, who plays in the Youth Orchestra, is one of the many orchestral players who teach children in the townships. It’s a way of promoting the hobby and could one day provide them with a job, should they show promise.

Noluvuyo Nteta:
I understand the kids because each and every one of them come form different situations, so what I have and what I’ve been taught, I’ve always wanted to give back.

John Webb:
All the youth orchestras frequently play at various centers, like the V&A Waterfornt, where the Masidlale Group performed.

Noluvuyo Nteta:
I think for these kids, having the violin or playing the violin, is something that gives them hope for tomorrow or for the future.

John Webb:
One of their inspirations is Capetonian Brandon Phillips, who was acclaimed early this year in Berlin and Amsterdam.

Brandon Phillips:
I normally use a saying that music is the closest thing to heaven, it’s a taste of heaven.

John Webb:
He conducts the Youth Orchestra, as well as being the principal bassoonist in the Philharmonic itself. He runs a tight ship.

Brandon Phillips:
There is no mistakes, I don’t accept mistakes. It’s Russian school technique type of, you know Russian, very strict, no mistakes.

John Webb:
Brandon has watched his friend, Dane Coetzee, rapidly progress after joining the Youth Orchestra in 2004. His mastery of his cello has allowed him to even at times play in the professional orchestra.

Dane Coetzee:
I’m still on my journey, but I know what impact the system has had for my life.

John Webb:
Brandon’s greatest joy is seeing how he can coax the very best out of his charges for their live performances.

Brandon Phillips:
To see them smile, to hear them play, and after the concert, they are so happy, and they go home with this great smile, the face lights up.

John Webb:
Peter Klatzow has written a special piece called “Congratulations” and it’ll be performed by the Philharmonic at a special gala concert on the 4th of December to celebrate the centenary. A book about the illustrious history of Cape Town’s orchestras will be launched at this concert and should make all Capetonians very proud. Noluvuyo is proud to be part of celebrating 100 years of orchestral tradition in Cape Town. She is also excited about her role in transforming the Cape Town Philharmonic Orchestra.

Noluvuyo Nteta:
If you would have the whole orchestra spread out in the different townships that we have in Cape Town, it would be life changing for everyone. And everyone would come together and speak one language.
